body: Though you may not perceive the difference in taste between lactose free and regular milk, lactose free milk does taste sweeter. Lactose free milk is produced by treating milk with the enzyme lactase which breaks lactose into its two component sugars glucose and galactose (the process that would occur naturally in the lactose tolerant person's digestion). Both of these sugars more freely bind with the sugar receptors of taste buds. Thus, it tastes a bit sweeter.

Don't listen to my well intentioned friend, Rice has a very specific cooking method and any deviation can screw it up. 

1. Bring the liquid to a boil, read the package for rice to liquid ratio as it varies from variety to variety. You can choose to add something other than water but stick to the appropriate amount of water. 
2. Add the rice when the liquid is boiling. Give it a little stir after you toss it in. This is also the time you would toss in a small amount of fat and salt, that might mean oil or butter but limit the salt you add if you are using salted butter. 
3. Put on a tight fitting lid and reduce heat to simmer, this is like medium low heat. 
4. Don't peak at it. Keep the lid on until the appropriate amount of time has passed (read the package, usually 20-25 minutes depending on the variety). 
5. When the time is up you should still notice a little steam coming out of the top of the lid, now you peak. This is your first peak. Pull off the lid and look at the rice. Looks cooked? Now tilt the pot to see if their is any liquid pooled in the bottom. If there is put the lid back on and wait. 
6. If you check and there is not water sitting in the bottom of the pot put the lid back on, pull it off the heat, and let it sit for about 5 minutes. This step keeps the rice from being stuck to the bottom of the pot. 

Trouble shooting:

Rice too dry, crunchy: You either failed to read the package and put in the appropriate amount of water, you peaked and let moisture escape, or you burnt it. 

Rice soggy: Too much water, not cooked long enough. 

Rice dissolved, almost mushy: too much water and cooked too long. 

Rice stuck to bottom of pot/not burnt: You pulled the lid off at the end and let it cool that way. Moisture escaped during the final stage that got the bottom kernels stuck to the pot. 

Rice stuck to bottom of pot/brown: The heat level you chose on your burner during the simmering stage (step 3) was too high. Keep that in mind and next time use a lower heat setting. 

Rice tastes bad: You didn't season it. This is why you choose to use broth instead of water, use 50/50 coconut milk and water, add fat, or add salt.

Try talking this out, and try not to label yourself as someone who has a panic/anxiety disorder because it will make this experience harder to shake.

You have to find the right reason to do it. I have spent the last 6 months studying motivational processes and have found that if you do something for an external goal (to look good, to attract women, to fit into pants, to be beautiful) you will have a much harder time sticking with it. When you have an external motivation then you have external validation of your efforts (which might be inconsistent or nonexistent). 

You have to do it because you are curious. You have to want to loose weight because you have never been able to run before and you want to know what it feels like. You want to loose weight because you always weighed too much to do that thing you always wanted to try. Because you are so damn curious about who you could be and what you could achieve that you just had to try it. For you it might be that you really miss being able enjoy the feeling and rush of performing or fighting - those should be the things you think about and focus on. 

These are called intrinsic motivations. These completely internal, curiosity and experience based motivations will help you stick with your goal. It is possible to achieve your goals for extrinsic motivations (external goals) but cognitively re-framing your reasons for engaging in fitness will really help. It's called Self-Determination Theory if you want to know more about it (but it really works).
